items.text: We propose structural scaffolds, a multitask model to incorporate structural information of scientiﬁc papers into citations for effective classiﬁcation of citation intents.
items.why: States the proposed method.
items.plain: We introduce structural scaffolds, a model that learns multiple tasks at once to add structural information from research articles to citations for citation intent classification.

items.text: Our model achieves a new state-ofthe-art on an existing ACL anthology dataset (ACL-ARC) with a 13.3% absolute increase in F1 score, without relying on external linguistic resources or hand-engineered features as done in existing methods.
items.why: Summarizes the main quantitative improvement on ACL-ARC.
items.plain: Our model achieves a new best result on the ACL Anthology dataset with a 13.3% higher overall F1 score, without using external language resources or manually designed features.

items.text: In addition, we introduce a new dataset of citation intents (Sci- Cite) which is more than ﬁve times larger and covers multiple scientiﬁc domains compared with existing datasets.
items.why: Describes the key properties of SciCite dataset.
items.plain: We introduce Sci-Cite, a new dataset for citation intent that is over five times larger and spans several scientific fields compared to existing datasets.

items.text: In particular, we propose two auxiliary tasks as structural scaffolds to improve citation intent prediction:1 (1) predicting the section title in which the citation occurs and (2) predicting whether a sentence needs a citation.
items.why: Defines the specific auxiliary scaffold tasks.
items.plain: We propose two secondary tasks as structural scaffolds to support intent prediction: predicting which section heading a citation appears in, and predicting whether a sentence needs a citation.

We encode the tokens in the citation context of size n as x = {x1, ..., xn}, where xi ∈Rd1 is a word vector of size d1 which concatenates non-contextualized word representations (GloVe, Pennington et al., 2014) and contextualized embeddings (ELMo, Peters et al., 2018), i.e.:
items.why: Explains initial token embedding setup.
items.plain: We convert each word token in an n-word citation context into a vector by combining static GloVe embeddings and contextual ELMo embeddings.

items.text: We then use a bidirectional long short-term memory (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) (BiL- STM) network with hidden size of d2 to obtain a contextual representation of each token vector with respect to the entire sequence:2
items.why: Describes sequence encoding with BiLSTM.
items.plain: We then pass the token vectors through a bidirectional long short-term memory network to create context-aware representations across the entire sentence.

items.text: We then use an attention mechanism to get a single vector representing the whole input sequence:
items.why: Explains context aggregation via attention.
items.plain: We use an attention mechanism to combine the sequence of hidden states into a single vector for the entire input sequence.

items.text: where w is a parameter served as the query vector for dot-product attention.3 So far we have obtained the citation representation as a vector z.
items.why: Defines vector notation z for sentence representation.
items.plain: A vector w serves as a learnable query to calculate dot-product attention, yielding the final citation representation vector z.

items.text: The ﬁrst scaffold task that we consider is “citation worthiness” of a sentence, indicating whether a sentence needs a citation.
items.why: Defines the first scaffold task.
items.plain: The first secondary task is predicting citation worthiness, which determines if a given sentence requires a citation.

items.text: To this end, using citation markers such as “[12]” or “Lee et al (2010)”, we identify sentences in a paper that include citations and the negative samples are sentences without citation markers.
items.why: Details dataset creation for citation worthiness.
items.plain: We treat sentences with citation markers like [12] as positive examples and sentences without citation markers as negative examples.

items.text: The second scaffold task relates to predicting the section title in which a citation appears.
items.why: Defines the second scaffold task.
items.plain: The second secondary task predicts the section heading under which a citation is written.

items.text: We are using the section titles from a larger set of data than training data for the main task as a proxy to learn linguistic patterns that are helpful for citation intents.
items.why: Explains why section prediction works without manually engineered input features.
items.plain: We use section headings from a larger dataset to help the model learn linguistic patterns relevant to citation intent, rather than adding section titles directly as input features.

items.text: tion and the parameters for the lower layers of the network are shared across tasks.
items.why: Explains standard parameter sharing across tasks.
items.plain: Each secondary task uses its own task-specific parameters at top layers, while lower layer network parameters are shared across all tasks.

items.text: We use a Multi Layer Perceptron (MLP) for each task and then a softmax layer to obtain prediction probabilites.
items.why: Defines task output head architecture.
items.plain: We pass shared representations into a multilayer perceptron for each task, followed by a softmax layer to output class probabilities.

items.text: In particular, given the vector z we pass it to n MLPs and obtain n output vectors y(i):
items.why: Formalizes MLP mapping from context vector.
items.plain: Given representation z, we pass it into n distinct multi-layer perceptrons to obtain n output vectors.

items.text: We are only interested in the output y(1) and the rest of outputs (y(2), ..., y(n)) are regarding the scaffold tasks and only used in training to inform the model of knowledge in the structure of the scientiﬁc documents.
items.why: Clarifies main vs secondary task inference.
items.plain: We only keep the main task output during final prediction; secondary outputs are used solely during training to teach document structure.

items.text: Similarly, let L1 and Li be the main loss and the loss of the auxiliary task i, respectively.
items.why: Gives loss function notation.
items.plain: The overall training loss combines the main classification loss L1 and individual secondary task losses Li.

items.text: where λi is a hyper-parameter specifying the sensitivity of the parameters of the model to each speciﬁc task.
items.why: Defines multi-task weighting hyperparameter.
items.plain: The parameter lambda_i determines how much weight each specific task has during model parameter updates.

items.text: In each training epoch, we construct mini-batches with the same number of instances from each of the n tasks.
items.why: Describes batch creation for multi-task learning.
items.plain: In each training epoch, mini-batches contain equal numbers of samples from each of the n tasks.

items.text: We compute the total loss for each mini-batch as described in Equation 1, where Li=0 for all instances of other tasks j̸=i.
items.why: Explains loss evaluation per instance.
items.plain: We calculate total mini-batch loss using Equation 1, setting loss to 0 for tasks other than the task a given instance belongs to.

items.text: We compute the gradient of the loss for each mini-batch and tune model parameters using the AdaDelta optimizer (Zeiler, 2012) with gradient clipping threshold of 5.0.
items.why: States optimizer, clipping, and update choices.
items.plain: We compute gradients for each mini-batch and update parameters using AdaDelta with gradient clipping set to 5.0.

items.text: We stop training the model when the development macro F1 score does not improve for ﬁve consecutive epochs.
items.why: States early stopping criterion.
items.plain: We stop training when macro F1 score on validation data stops improving for five straight epochs.

items.text: In addition, to address the limited scope and size of this dataset, we introduce SciCite, a new dataset of citation intents that addresses multiple scientiﬁc domains and is more than ﬁve times larger than ACL-ARC.
items.why: Summarizes SciCite size and domain reach.
items.plain: We introduce SciCite, a citation intent dataset covering several fields of science that is over five times larger than ACL-ARC.

items.text: The dataset is based on a sample of papers from the ACL Anthology Reference Corpus (Bird et al., 2008) and includes 1,941 citation instances from 186 papers and is annotated by domain experts in the NLP ﬁeld.
items.why: Details sample size and domain of ACL-ARC.
items.plain: ACL-ARC contains 1,941 annotated citations taken from 186 papers in natural language processing.

items.text: The data was split into three standard stratiﬁed sets of train, validation, and test with 85% of data used for training and remaining 15% divided equally for validation and test.
items.why: Details train/val/test splits for ACL-ARC.
items.plain: The dataset is split into training (85%), validation (7.5%), and test (7.5%) sets.

items.text: The data includes six intent categories outlined in Table 2.
items.why: States number of intent categories in ACL-ARC.
items.plain: The dataset contains six citation intent classes.

items.text: We consider three intent categories outlined in Table 1: BACK-
items.why: Defines the three classes in SciCite.
items.plain: SciCite categorizes citations into three main intent classes: Background, Method, and Result comparison.

items.text: Citation intent of sentence extractions was labeled through the crowdsourcing platform Figure Eight.6 We selected a sample of papers from the Semantic Scholar corpus,7 consisting of papers in general computer science and medicine domains.
items.why: Describes corpus source for SciCite.
items.plain: We collected citation context samples from computer science and medicine papers in the Semantic Scholar corpus and annotated them via Figure Eight.

items.text: parse.8 The annotators were asked to identify the intent of a citation, and were directed to select among three citation intent options: METHOD, RESULTCOMPARISON and BACKGROUND.
items.why: Details annotation task options presented to workers.
items.plain: Annotators assigned citation contexts into standard classes: METHOD, RESULTCOMPARISON, or BACKGROUND.

items.text: We later removed instances annotated with the OTHER option from our dataset (less than 1% of the annotated data), many of which were due to citation contexts which are incomplete or too short for the annotator to infer the citation intent.
items.why: Explains filtering of OTHER category.
items.plain: We removed items marked as OTHER (under 1% of the annotations), which mostly contained incomplete or very short contexts.

items.text: To only collect high quality annotations, instances with conﬁdence score of ≤0.7 were discarded.
items.why: Gives dataset confidence threshold filtering rule.
items.plain: We dropped annotated items whose inter-annotator confidence score was 0.7 or lower.

items.text: In addition, a subset of the dataset with 100 samples was re-annotated by a trained, expert annotator to check for quality, and the agreement rate with crowdsource workers was 86%.
items.why: Reports expert agreement rate on SciCite crowd annotations.
items.plain: An expert re-annotated 100 samples, reaching an 86% agreement rate with crowdsourced workers.

items.text: This resulted in a total 9,159 crowdsourced instances which were divided to training and validation sets with 90% of the data used for the training set.
items.why: States crowdsourced dataset split for SciCite.
items.plain: Crowdsourcing produced 9,159 valid instances, split into 90% training and 10% validation sets.

items.text: In addition to the crowdsourced data, a separate test set of size 1,861 was annotated by a trained, expert annotator to ensure high quality of the dataset.
items.why: Details expert-annotated test set size.
items.plain: We created a separate expert-annotated test set containing 1,861 instances.

items.text: We also remove the citation markers from those sentences
items.why: Explains critical preprocessing to prevent citation worthiness data leakage.
items.plain: We remove inline citation text like [1] or Lee et al. (2012) so the model cannot rely on explicit markers.

items.text: We manually deﬁne regular expression patterns mappings to normalized section titles: “introduction”, “related work”, “method”, “experiments”, “conclusion”.
items.why: Explains normalization of section titles into 5 canonical classes.
items.plain: We mapped section headers to five canonical titles using regular expressions: introduction, related work, method, experiments, and conclusion.

items.text: Overall, the size of the data for scaffold tasks on the ACL-ARC dataset is about 47K (section title scaffold) and 50K (citation worthiness) while on SciCite is about 91K and 73K for section title and citation worthiness scaffolds, respectively.
items.why: Gives dataset sizes for auxiliary task datasets.
items.plain: Auxiliary datasets contain 47K section title and 50K worthiness samples for ACL-ARC, and 91K section title and 73K worthiness samples for SciCite.

items.text: For word representations, we use 100-dimensional GloVe vectors (Pennington et al., 2014) trained on a corpus of 6B tokens from Wikipedia and Gigaword.
items.why: Specifies word vector parameters.
items.plain: We use 100-dimensional GloVe vectors pre-trained on Wikipedia and Gigaword corpora.

items.text: For contextual representations, we use ELMo vectors released by Peters et al. (2018)10
items.why: Specifies contextual vector parameters.
items.plain: We use ELMo embeddings with 1,024 dimensions pre-trained on 5.5 billion words.

items.text: We use a single-layer BiLSTM with a hidden dimension size of 50 for each direction11.
items.why: States BiLSTM architecture dimensions.
items.plain: We use a single-layer BiLSTM network with 50 hidden units per direction.

items.text: For each of scaffold tasks, we use a single-layer MLP with 20 hidden nodes , ReLU (Nair and Hinton, 2010) activation and a Dropout rate (Srivastava et al., 2014) of 0.2 between the hidden and input layers.
items.why: Details MLP scaffold layers and hyperparameters.
items.plain: Each secondary task head consists of a single MLP layer with 20 hidden units, ReLU activations, and a 0.2 dropout rate.

items.text: The hyperparameters λi are tuned for best performance on the validation set of the respective datasets using a 0.0 to 0.3 grid search.
items.why: States tuning method for loss weights.
items.plain: Loss weight parameters lambda_i were selected by searching values from 0.0 to 0.3 on validation data.

items.text: Citation worthiness saffold: λ2=0.08, λ3=0, section title scaffold: λ3=0.09, λ2=0; both scaffolds: λ2=0.1, λ3=0.05.
items.why: Gives selected hyperparameter values for ACL-ARC.
items.plain: For ACL-ARC, the best settings were lambda_2=0.08 for worthiness alone, lambda_3=0.09 for section title alone, and lambda_2=0.1, lambda_3=0.05 when combining both.

items.text: Batch size is 8 for ACL-ARC dataset and 32 for SciCite dataset (recall that SciCite is larger than ACL-ARC).
items.why: States batch size per dataset.
items.plain: Mini-batch size was set to 8 for ACL-ARC and 32 for SciCite.

items.text: This baseline uses a similar architecture to our proposed neural multitask learning framework, except that it only optimizes the network for the main loss regarding the citation intent classiﬁcation (L1) and does not include the structural scaffolds.
items.why: Defines baseline model structure for ablation comparison.
items.plain: The primary baseline uses the same network architecture but is trained strictly on main task intent loss without scaffold tasks.

items.text: Our implementation of this model achieves a macro-averaged F1 score of 0.526 using 10-fold cross-validation, which is in line with the highest reported results in Jurgens et al. (2018): 0.53 using leave-oneout cross validation.
items.why: Confirms baseline replication quality for prior SOTA.
items.plain: Our re-implementation of Jurgens et al. (2018) achieved a 0.526 macro F1 score, matching its published performance.

items.text: BiLSTM-Attn + section title scaffold 56.9 BiLSTM-Attn + citation worthiness scaffold 56.3 BiLSTM-Attn + both scaffolds 63.1 BiLSTM-Attn w/ ELMo + both scaffolds 67.9
items.why: Reports ablation and full model results on ACL-ARC dataset.
items.plain: On ACL-ARC, macro F1 increases from 51.8 baseline to 56.9 with section titles, 56.3 with worthiness, 63.1 with both scaffolds, and 67.9 when adding ELMo embeddings.

items.text: When both scaffolds are used simultaneously in ‘BiLSTM-Attn + both scaffolds’, the F1 score further improves to 63.1 (∆=11.3), suggesting that the two tasks provide complementary signal that is useful for citation intent prediction.
items.why: Shows complementary performance gain of using both scaffolds.
items.plain: Combining both auxiliary tasks increases macro F1 to 63.1, showing that the two tasks provide complementary learning signals.

items.text: The best result is achieved when we also add ELMo vectors (Peters et al., 2018) to the input representations in ‘BiLSTM-Attn w/ ELMo + both scaffolds’, achieving an F1 of 67.9, a major improvement from the previous state-of-the-art results of Jurgens et al. (2018) 54.6 (∆=13.3).
items.why: Highlights final improvement over prior SOTA on ACL-ARC.
items.plain: Adding ELMo embeddings to both scaffolds yields a peak F1 of 67.9, surpassing the previous state of the art by 13.3 F1 points.

items.text: We note that the scaffold tasks provide major contributions on top of the ELMo-enabled baseline (∆=13.6), demonstrating the efﬁcacy of using structural scaffolds for citation intent prediction.
items.why: Isolates the performance boost given by scaffolds over ELMo baseline.
items.plain: Auxiliary scaffold tasks add a 13.6 point F1 improvement over the baseline that already includes ELMo embeddings.

items.text: We also experimented with adding features used in Jurgens et al. (2018) to our best model and not only we did not see any improvements, but we observed
items.why: Evaluates combining manual features with neural model.
items.plain: Adding manual features from previous work to our top neural model failed to improve classification performance.

items.text: BiLSTM-Attn + section title scaffold 77.8 BiLSTM-Attn + citation worthiness scaffold 78.1 BiLSTM-Attn + both scaffolds 79.1 BiLSTM-Attn w/ ELMo + both scaffolds 84.0
items.why: Reports ablation and full model results on SciCite dataset.
items.plain: On SciCite, macro F1 improves from 77.2 baseline to 77.8 with section titles, 78.1 with worthiness, 79.1 with both scaffolds, and 84.0 with ELMo plus both scaffolds.

items.text: Therefore, suggesting the effectiveness the scaffolds in informing the main task of relevant signals for citation intent classiﬁcation.
items.why: Confirms scaffold multi-tasking causes structural attention changes.
items.plain: Because structural scaffolds are the only difference from the baseline, they account for the observed focus on intent-bearing words.

items.text: One general error pattern is that the model has more tendency to make false positive errors in the BACKGROUND category likely due to this category dominating both datasets.
items.why: Notes main classification error pattern across datasets.
items.plain: The model frequently misclassifies rare categories as Background because Background is the majority class in both datasets.

items.text: We experimented with encoding the extended surrounding context using a BiLSTM and concatenating it with the main citation context vector (z), but it resulted in a large decline in overall performance likely due to the overall noise introduced by the additional context.
items.why: Reports negative experiment outcome of extending context representations.
items.plain: Concatenating wider surrounding text embeddings encoded via BiLSTM degraded overall performance due to added noise.

items.text: We propose a multitask learning framework with two auxiliary tasks (predicting section titles and citation worthiness) as two scaffolds related to the main task of citation intent prediction.
items.why: Summarizes the full multitask scaffold system setup.
items.plain: We propose a multi-task learning architecture that uses section title and citation worthiness tasks as auxiliary scaffolds for intent classification.

items.text: Our model achieves state-of-the-art result (F1 score of 67.9%) on the ACL-ARC dataset with 13.3 absolute increase over the best previous results.
items.why: Restates final ACL-ARC evaluation claim.
items.plain: Our model achieves a 67.9% F1 score on ACL-ARC, outperforming the prior benchmark by 13.3 percentage points.
